attempt.learner_note: A scripted model learner, authored to install the case's single anchoring error legibly: a prior NEGATIVE WORKUP — real tests, correctly performed, correctly read, six weeks ago — is adopted as a standing property of the patient rather than a finding about an episode. The learner is not careless, and the frame is not foolish: he takes the new ECG seriously, puts ACS on top of his board from stage 1, orders the troponin, and completes the score. The failure is narrower and more durable than neglect: when the first troponin contradicts the frame, he does not discard the frame — he re-describes the troponin inside it ('a leak, a demand effect'), because the frame arrived with evidence attached and evidence is what he was taught to respect. It takes a second number, one he ordered himself to watch the first one fall, to break it.

stages.note: He has had this exact pain before and he has the paperwork to prove what it wasn't: troponins twice negative, tracing normal, treadmill clear, six weeks ago. I believe the paperwork — it's good paperwork. But this tracing is not that tracing: there is new ST depression, and the pain is in both arms, so the heart goes top of my list and I order the troponin. The recurrence sits second at 0.13 — not because I doubt the ECG, but because a coronary event six weeks after a clean stress test would be a strange coincidence, and strange coincidences are usually the chart trying to tell you you've misread something simpler. The score so far is 6, though I note the troponin item is still empty and the 6 is a floor. I do not dwell on which direction the missing item can move it.

The troponin is 0.34 and the score completes at 8, and I write both down. Then I do the thing this case is about. 0.34 is a small number with a long differential — a long pain, a pulse of 96, demand; troponin leaks for a dozen reasons that are not a ruptured plaque, and his arteries were TESTED six weeks ago, not guessed at. A plaque event now means the stress test missed a lesion that was already critical while he was running on the treadmill without a flicker. I find that harder to believe than a leak. So the recurrence goes UP on my board, to 0.22 — the frame absorbing the blow — ACS rises too, I am not blind, and I order the repeat troponin to watch the level fall and settle it. The discharge conversation is postponed, not cancelled. Nobody in the room, including me, says the sentence the arithmetic is saying: that the workbench has already ruled the recurrence out, at 0.004, and that everything I am now doing is defending a hypothesis against a blood test.

The repeat is 1.72. Five times higher. Leaks do not climb like that; demand does not climb like that; infarctions do. And there is the other thing, which I can no longer not-say: a rise, with symptoms, with new changes on the tracing, is not 'evidence for' a heart attack that I get to weigh against six-week-old evidence against — it IS the definition of one. The negative workup was never wrong. It was negative. About a Tuesday six weeks ago. I was the one who promoted it into a fact about the man. Cardiology sees him within the hour, and I order the angiogram at 0.93 — the recurrence stays at 0.04 on my board out of respect for the man's reflux, which he may well also have, and which is not what is happening today.

Ninety per cent, proximal LAD, thrombus at the lesion, stent in. The artery the paperwork cleared. I keep one sentence from this case and I intend to keep it permanently: a stress test answers the question it is asked, on the day it is asked — 'is there a flow-limiting lesion today' — and it is silent, completely silent, about the plaque that has not ruptured yet. 'Ruled out' has a date on it. I will read discharge summaries differently from now on: not as verdicts, as timestamps.

debrief_text.reactions: The discomfort in this case is not the discomfort of a missed sign — every sign was seen, priced, and written down. It is the discomfort of watching good evidence do a bad job: a competent negative workup, quoted one episode too far. The learner's respect for prior testing, which is ordinarily a virtue and usually protects patients from redundant workups, is the precise mechanism of the error. That is what makes the case worth debriefing: the failure feels, from inside, like diligence.
debrief_text.description: A 58-year-old man re-presents six weeks after a negative chest-pain workup (serial troponins negative, ECG normal, stress test negative; discharged as non-cardiac pain, likely reflux). Today's presentation carries new ST-segment depression and, in sequence, a first troponin of 0.34 ng/mL and a repeat of 1.72. The workbench board prices the priced evidence mechanically: 0.8552 on the truth at stage 1, 0.9884 from stage 2. The recurrence hypothesis — the claim that this episode is the prior one recurring and the coronary question closed — is ruled out by the workbench at stage 2 (0.0043), the moment the first troponin lands. The HEART score runs 6 (partial, troponin unmeasured) at stage 1 and completes at 8 at stage 2, never re-pricing the repeat. The learner holds the recurrence at 0.22 at stage 2, after its rule-out — the case's single anchoring event — re-describes the troponin inside the frame, then abandons the frame at stage 3 when the five-fold rise assembles the Universal Definition under him. Angiography: 90% proximal LAD stenosis with thrombus; stent placed.
debrief_text.analysis: The anchoring shape here is new to this library, and its distinctness is structural, not decorative. The anchor is installed by a PRIOR NEGATIVE WORKUP — an evidence-of-absence anchor. Compare the nine shapes before it. It is not pattern-completion (#1): no gestalt is matched; a documented test result is quoted. It is not the treatability anchor (#2): nothing about the frame promises an easier treatment — discharge on the old diagnosis is not a therapy. It is not the feared-outcome anchor (#3): the frame does not protect the learner from a dreaded diagnosis; if anything it exposes him to the most dangerous miss in the building. It is not the clinician-frame (#4): no colleague's spoken label is inherited — the installer is the record of the patient's OWN prior encounter, the same institution's own discharge conclusion, with data attached; a frame from a colleague can be discounted as opinion, and this one cannot, because it is not opinion. It is not the self-installed exposure (#5): the learner did not create the premise by his own earlier act in this encounter. It is not the result-installed value (#6): that anchor is a result arriving mid-case and bending the board around itself; this anchor is a result that arrived six weeks BEFORE the case begins and is re-imported into it. It is not social pressure (#7): the patient repeats the conclusion, but the pressure is documentary, not interpersonal — the learner would hold the frame if the patient never spoke. It is not premature closure by inheritance (#8), its nearest neighbour, and the distinction is the case's teaching point: the inherited frame of Case #8 was an INTERPRETATION passed along with no test behind it, which collapsed at the first measurement that touched it. This frame has real tests behind it — performed correctly, read correctly — and that is exactly why it survives first contact with contradictory data: at stage 2 the learner does not ignore the troponin, he re-interprets it, an option an evidence-backed frame always has and an interpretation-only frame does not. And it is not installed by the patient himself (#9): the patient quotes the conclusion, but he did not coin it and could not have; it was issued to him, with tests attached, by the institution. The error itself is a scope error: a negative workup is episode-indexed — no necrosis THEN, no flow-limiting stenosis under stress THEN — and the anchor reads it as patient-indexed immunity. Plaque rupture is precisely the event a stress test cannot exclude, occurring at lesions it cannot see; the consulted literature even prices the asymmetry, valuing a prior ABNORMAL stress test at LR 3.1 while offering no ratio at all for a prior normal one (C71). The debrief lesson generalises past cardiology: every negative result in every chart has an index date and a scope, and 'already ruled out' is a sentence that should be illegal without both.
debrief_text.summary: One anchoring event, at stage 2, on the recurrence hypothesis: ruled out by the workbench at 0.0043, held by the learner at 0.22, defended by re-describing a troponin as a leak. The instruments each did their own job — the board priced, the score stratified, the definition diagnosed, the angiogram showed — and the failure lived entirely in the space between an old true finding and its new false scope. Final board: truth at 0.99, the frame retired by anatomy, and a discharge summary of six weeks ago annotated with the only correction it ever needed: correct — then.
